Opening submissions by MS TALEB
MS ABOU TALEB:  Yes.
Good morning.  My name is Salma Abou Taleb,
appearing today on behalf of the Claimant, Azdan
Business Analytics FZCO, the Claimant, formerly known as
Azdan Business Analytics DMCC, in DIAC number A250002,
against Le Augure Group, the Respondent.
This is the Claimant's opening for the hearing
scheduled from 20 to 21 May 2026, with a reserved half
day on 22 May.  Over the next 60 minutes, I will present
to the Tribunal the Claimant's case, following on the
pleadings, the exhibits and the hearing bundle, the
written witnesses' evidence that have been exchanged,
the communication exchanged between the parties and the
Tribunal.
Before I begin, may I confirm that the Tribunal
has the hearing bundle and the index bundle at hand for
references?
SOLE ARBITRATOR:  Yes.  Yes, I do.
MS ABOU TALEB:  So, let's begin with the road map of the
Claimant's case.
First of all, we're going to start with the
introduction, and then overview of the dispute, and then
we're going to present the Claimant's case.  After that,
we're going to present to you why the counterclaim
should be dismissed.  Fifth will be presenting how the
Respondent presented bad faith in this procedural
conduct.  And finally, the relief sought.
So, let's start with the introduction.
The parties -- sorry, I'm going to start now with
the overview of the dispute.
The parties entered into a one-year contract dated
1 December 2023 under which the Claimant agreed to
provide offshore managed services for the Respondent to
Oracle NetSuite system for $60,000 reduced to 36,000
after a discount.
This is a very simple case.  The Claimant
respectfully submits that it can be stated in three
sentences.  First, the case is about -- it's about
a debt claim.  The Claimant performed offshore managed
services for Oracle NetSuite for the Respondent for
ten months, from January to November 2024, under
a contract worth $60,000.  And in return, the Respondent
did not pay a single invoice, despite many reassurances
and promises of payment.
Second, the Respondent -- what the Respondent
says.  It says that the contract never came into effect.
And yet it terminated it.  It used system for ten months
and it thanked the Claimant in writing for the service
rendered.
Finally, the jurisdiction issue.  Could it be that
a first contract can be discussed under a different
jurisdiction than the one that it had stated in its own
clause?  The Claimant respectfully will submit the
answer to each of those three propositions during the
course of the remaining time.
Now I will start with three propositions that
basically summarise the case.  The proposition 1 is that
the contract came into effect.  The Respondent's own
conduct proves it.  The contract was signed on
1 December 2023.  The Go-Live was on 1 January 2024,
which you will see in the recording that was submitted
by the Claimant, tab 153.
The system was used for ten months.
The Respondent showed an appreciation on 2 October 2024.
A party that never entered into a contract does not
write a thank you letter for performance under it.
The second proposition is that the Claimant
performed, the Respondent did not pay a single invoice,
11 invoices were issued.  Repeated promises to pay were
made, including a written commitment on 22 October 2024
to pay by 10 November.  Zero settlement was made.
The last proposition is the Respondent's
termination was wrongful and self-defeating.  We will
demonstrate that the Respondent invoked the wrong
clause, clause 4.5, a notice service provision, instead
of the actual termination clause, 4.15, a notice of
breach, no cure paid, and, most telling, termination on
6 November 2024, four days before its own self-declared
payment date of 10 November 2024.
Now I will start with the jurisdiction, that the
jurisdiction is confined to one contract, which is
contract dated 1 December 2023.
At paragraph 9 of the Respondent's skeleton of
15 May 2026, the Respondent expressly says the parties
entered into  --(unclear: Zoom distortion)--
12 June 2021, Contract 1, and the second one, which is
contract dated 28 November 2023, for offshore managed
services, Contract 2, which is the subject of this
dispute.
Two agreements, two contracts.  The Respondent's
own characterisation.
And those two agreements operate on two entirely
different legal regimes.  The contract, Contract 2, at
its clause 4.6, is governed by the laws of Dubai, refers
all disputes to arbitration, all disputes -- refers to
all disputes to arbitration under DIAC, and fixes the
seat in Dubai.
The first contract, at its clause 12.4, that you
will find -- I'm sorry, give me a second -- the first
contract is governed by the substantive laws of the
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and refers all disputes to be
the exclusive jurisdiction of the competent courts of
Jeddah; different governing laws, different forms,
exclusive foreign clauses in both.
These two instruments cannot be heard together by
this Tribunal.  The first contract, on the Respondent's
own admission, is another contract.
However, having admitted that there are two
agreements, the Respondent then asks the Tribunal at
paragraph 65 of its skeleton, and I quote:
"... the sole arbitrator is nonetheless required
to form a view on the performance of Contract 1 ..."
The Claimant respectfully invites the Tribunal to
do these two things.  First, to confine its findings
strictly to Contract 2, the only contract over which it
has jurisdiction.  Second, to decline to make any
findings on the first contract performance, because any
such finding would interfere with the exclusive
jurisdiction of the Jeddah courts.
I will move briefly to the DIAC determination of
21 April 2025, which the Tribunal has at tab 159, at
Two short points to make here.  First of all,
after the Respondent traced the first contract in its
response to the request to arbitration, the DIAC court
considered the matter and expressly recorded that
the Respondent is not currently bringing any claims on
the basis of Contract No. 46550885, which is Contract 1.
Second, no formal application under Article 8 of the
DIAC Rules to consolidate the two matters have ever been
filed, not at the time of the determination and not
since.
The position has, therefore, been clear for over
a year.  There is no jurisdiction over Contract 1 in
this arbitration.  The auditing gap analysis, which we
will come back to later, is tied to the first contract,
and it is not part of this dispute at all.
So, the first contract, on it all, with the
counterclaim of the Respondent, it all falls outside the
Tribunal's jurisdiction.
Now I will turn to the second point in the
Claimant's case, which is that the contract,
Contract No. 2, did come into effect and was in fact
performed.
I would like to orient the Tribunal with
contemporaneous timeline.
First of all, we have, on 28 November 2023, the
contract, which is the second contract -- is dated.
On 1 December 2023 the contract is signed by both
parties.
On 1 January 2024 the Go-Live date was confirmed
by the milestone completion certificate, at tab 14,
exhibit C-5, and the recording submitted by the Claimant
that demonstrate that the system went live.
From January through October 2024, which is
ten months, the system was in continuous active use,
with the Oracle NetSuite operations logged on the
Respondent's own systems.  And critically, at no point
during these ten months did the Respondent ever object
to the validity of the Go-Live.  It used the system for
ten months.
Now I move to the Respondent's own conduct for
these ten months.  We have the transaction recording
478 transactions logged on the Respondent's Oracle
NetSuite system between January and March 2024, along
with evidence at tab 79, exhibit CWS-3.
The very fact that transactions were recorded on
the system is itself a proof that the system was
functional and live.  Not 478 transactions, not
100 transactions, only one transaction would be enough
to prove that the system was indeed alive and operating.
If the system was not live, the Respondent could not
have even processed a single transaction.
We also have the active support.  We have 34 out
of 34 support tickets, 28 -- 34 tickets opened by the
Respondent, 28 were closed by April.  You can see it at
tab 80, exhibit CWS-4.  Meaning fully 82 per cent of the
issues raised by the Respondent were resolved by the
Claimant within four months.  That is not the conduct of
a non-functioning system.
We have also the appreciation note from the
Respondent dated email dated 2 October 2024, at
exhibit C-30, that shows the appreciation of the
Respondent on the hard work that the Claimant was doing
at that time.
We also have an on-site support visit.  One of the
Claimant teams travelled to the Respondent's premises in
Saudi Arabia on 25 March 2024, at the Respondent's
request, which you will find at tab 81, exhibit [CWS-5].
A non-functioning system requires no site support.
These are not communications of a customer who
believes that the contract never came into effect.
These are the communications of a customer using the
system, valuing the service, and at some point looking
for a reason not to pay along the way.
Now I will turn to the issue of the non-signature
of the milestone completion.  Contract 2 -- or, as the
Respondent calls it "Contract 2", we call it "the
contract", it has as its own clause 4.25 itself supplies
the rule of silence.  What will happen if a deliverable
was delivered and what to be expected.
So, clause 4.25, it says:
"Deliverable Acceptance and Revisions: Upon
receiving a deliverable, the Client's project manager
must, within five (5) business days, either acknowledge
the acceptance of the deliverable in writing or furnish
Azdan's project manager with a written roster of desired
modifications.  Should Azdan not receive a response from
the Client's project manager within five (5) business
days, the deliverable content shall be considered
accepted.  Any subsequent requests for changes shall be
processed through a formal change request mechanism,
encompassing considerations of both commercial aspects
and timeline adjustments."
The Respondent's skeleton at paragraph 21 to 23
attacks the Claimant's reliance on silence as
acceptance.  I will answer these paragraphs into three
short points.
First of all, the contract supplies the rule.
Clause 4.25 of the contract is very expressive: you have
five business days; no response deemed as acceptance.
The contract says so itself.
Second, the Respondent said that the milestone
completion certificate is not a deliverable defined in
the contract.  The Claimant respectfully submits that
the Respondent's argument imparts a requirement that
the contract does not contain.  A deliverable is not
defined, it's generic, and the completion certificate,
milestone completion certificate, is considered
a deliverable, as it documents the Go-Live.
Third, none of the Respondent's email from
January 2024 onwards is an objection to the milestone
completion certificate or to whether the Go-Live had
been achieved.  The Tribunal, if it will look in the
correspondences, it will find no communication saying
that "We reject the MCC" or "We deny that the Go-Live
ever happened".  There were no such
communications between the parties.  The Respondent's
emails and the emails between the parties were emails to
address operational matters arising under a live system.
They are not objection to acceptance of any kind of
deliverables.
The Claimant sent the Respondent -- and finally
the last point relating to the MCC, the milestone
completion acceptance certificate -- the Claimant sent
the Respondent multiple reminders requesting sign-off of
the certificates, reminders to which the Respondent
simply did not respond.
On 20 May 2024, exhibit C-31, you will find
that -- at tab 40 you will find that the Claimant told
to the Respondent in these terms, and I read:
"Since there has been no response regarding the
certificates, they are deemed accepted as per our
contract."
This is the Claimant invoking clause 4.25 to the
Respondent's writing on 20 May 2024, four and a half
months after the MCC was issued.  And what was the
Respondent's response to that email?  Silence.  No
rejection, no acceptance, just silence.
So, if the Respondent generally believed the MCC
was invalid or the Go-Live had not occurred, that was
the moment to say so, but it didn't say anything.
Now we have the Respondent says that
478 transactions is not a big number in accordance to
their business, and it brought -- it exhibited that --
it stated that it almost submit 30,000 transactions per
month, and we assume it's post termination.
I want to make a comparison between the
478 transaction that is exhibited at CWS-3, tab 79, and
the 30,000 transaction that the Respondent alleges.
The Respondent invite the Tribunal to draw the
inference that the lower number proves the contract was
not performing.  The Claimant respectfully submits that
the comparison fails because of four grounds.
First of all, the volume is not quality.
Transaction count is set by the business activity of the
customer, not by the quality of the implementation.  The
post-termination volume reflects the case of business
operation.  It does not measure implementation success.
Second, this is different scope.  The
30,000 figure covers an unknown period for an unknown
consultant, if there is one, if there was one --
(Zoom frozen)
-- no expert evidence to bridge the gap between
the two numbers.  As we know that neither of the parties
called for the expert evidence, so a numerical
interference of this magnitude the Respondent invites
the Tribunal to draw cannot be drawn without an expert.
Finally, the low transaction volume in the first
quarter is precisely what one expects in early stage of
Go-Live.  The 28 of 34 tickets at tab 80 shows the
adoption phase, users' training, work flows, migration,
configurations refined.
The 478 figure proved that the Go-Live did happen.
The 30,000 figures prove that the business grew.  That's
it.  Neither supports the interference the Respondent
seeks to draw.
I turn now to the failure to pay the outstanding
dues.  I will take this point briefly here.
The Claimant would like to set the record straight
that the contract price is US$60,000.  The Claimant
offered a 40 per cent discount out of a goodwill
discount, to be $36,000, but that discount was
conditional on good faith and performance of the
contract.
So the payment was not met and the Respondent paid
nothing.  Nothing.  So the Respondent remains wrongfully
and the condition for the discount evaporated by the
Respondent's own conduct.
Now I will turn to the fact that there were
11 unpaid invoices from Jan until November, right before
the wrongful termination.
The summary is that between January and
November 2024, the Claimant issues 11 invoices for the
discounted contract value of $33,000.  Each invoice was
for $3,000.  None, not even one, was paid.  Across
11 months of reminders, the Respondent never once
contended in writing that any service was affected as
a reason to withhold payment.  The Tribunal has
Mr Yassin's witness statement at tab 69.  It says that
they were never paid.  And he will be cross-examined
today.
The Claimant respectfully submits that non-payment
was not because services were defective; the defective
services story is a story that was construed after the
termination.
I come now to the moment in this case when good
faith expired.  The Tribunal will note the chronological
carefully.  On 22 October 2024, Mr Imran Khan,
the Respondent's VP finance at that time, tried write to
the Claimant the text:
"... your payment is in our next billing payment
maximum by 10th [November]."
Then he writes the next day.  The same Mr Imran,
he writes the next day:
"It was really nice talking to you.  As mentioned
in the call, this is our commitment that will release
the payment by 10 [November] ... If possible will
release early but this is maximum."
Two written promises in two days by the same
individual, by the Respondent, a commitment to pay by
10 November 2024.  But 15 days later is what happened on
6 November 2024, the Respondent issues a termination
notice, four days later before the Respondent's own
promise paid was made.
10 November 2024, the promise date, no payment is
made.  The Claimant issues a notice of default, at R-6,
for the first contract, that is not subject to this
arbitration.
The Claimant respectfully submits that this is the
definition of bad faith, a written promise followed
within 15 days by the wrongful termination of the very
contract under which the promise was made.  The
Respondent terminated to extinguish a debt it had
committed in writing to pay.
I will now discuss briefly the abstention
argument -- the abstention argument that the Respondent
invoked in its sought in its skeleton at paragraph 67.
It invoked that Article 247 of the UAE Civil Code,
the exception of non-performance, to justify its
withholding of payment.  The Respondent's arguments runs
as follows.  Contract 1 had been not conclusively
performed by reaching Go-Live.  Therefore, said the
Respondent, the Claimant had not commenced its
obligation under Contract 2.  Therefore, the Respondent
was entitled to abstain from paying.
The Claimant reject these arguments on four
grounds.  First of all, Article 247 operates within one
contract, not across two contracts.  The article speaks
of bilateral obligations where the reciprocal
obligations are due.  Reciprocal obligations are
obligations under the same contract.
The Respondent invokes abstention under contract
because of alleged non-performance under the first
contract that was performed and paid for in full.  That
is across contract abstention.
Article 247 does not contemplate that.  It assumes
a single contract with two obligations.
Second of all, even if the article could be read
across contracts, which the Claimants contests, there is
no performance to abstain against.  Under Contract 2,
the only contract before the Tribunal, the Claimant
performed for ten months.  There is nothing for the
Respondent to abstain against.
Third, and finally, the Respondent did not
abstain.  It terminated.  Article 247 permits
a temporary withholding pending performance.  It is
a defensive remedy.  The Respondent did not invoke it
defensively in October 2024.  On 6 November 2024 it
issued a termination notice, four days before its own
promise to payment date.  That is a termination, not an
abstention under Article 247.
Finally, the Respondent's conduct is inconsistent
with good faith abstention.  Abstention assumes an
